title: CIAM for AI: Authn/Authz for Agents — Michael Grinich, CEO of WorkOS

primary.label: Security, Safety, Identity & Governance

summary: The talk opens by framing CIAM as 'OAuth login for agents.' WorkOS's fastest-growing segment is AI companies. Grinich motivates the problem with a story of an IT support chatbot deleting a production database, showing how nondeterministic agents can cause destructive actions. Agents are a hybrid between machine and person identity. He explains why agent identity is hard: headless login with long-lived sessions, least-privilege tensions with nondeterministic agents, and compliance requiring audit trails tied to human owners. He proposes four architecture patterns: persona shadowing (scoped shadow identities), delegation chains (signed tokens passed step-by-step), capability tokens (time-bound vouchers for specific actions), and escalation to humans (with consent fatigue risk). He then surveys emerging standards. OAuth is ubiquitous but built for human consent and static scopes. UMA (User Managed Access) extends OAuth to let users externalize consent and access policies. GNAP enables dynamic negotiation of token scopes, valuable for agents needing unforeseen permissions, but lacks implementation. OIDC for Agents and W3C Verifiable Credentials are being adapted for agent identity claims and attestations. The dominant industry pattern is middleware—placing a managed trust boundary between agentic code and enterprise systems, since agents must be treated as untrusted. WorkOS offers OKIT for MCP identity and FGA for granular authorization. Grinich predicts traffic will flip from ~95% human to ~95% agent, drawing a ghost kitchen analogy. He calls for collaboration on agent identity standards.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

Agent identity is challenging due to headless login, dynamic permission needs, compliance, and observability requirements
Four architecture patterns—persona shadowing, delegation chains, capability tokens, and human escalation—can be combined depending on application needs
OAuth is ubiquitous but built for human consent and static scopes; UMA and GNAP extend or replace it for agent-specific needs
GNAP enables dynamic token scope negotiation but lacks real-world implementation
The dominant industry pattern is middleware—a managed trust boundary between agentic code and enterprise systems, treating agents as untrusted

Human-in-the-loop approval risks consent fatigue, reducing real security
Collaboration on new agent identity standards is urgently needed

sections.title: Introduction: Agents Need First-Class Identity
sections.summary: Grinich introduces CIAM for AI agents as 'OAuth login for agents.' WorkOS's fastest-growing segment is AI companies. He illustrates the problem with a story of an IT support agent deleting a production database, emphasizing that agents are only as powerful as the systems they access. Agents are a new paradigm needing first-class identity support—a hybrid of machine and person identity. He calls for collaboration on new agent identity standards.

sections.title: Why Agent Identity Is Hard
sections.summary: Agent identity is challenging because agents need headless login with long-lived sessions, raising credential storage and refresh questions. Least-privilege access conflicts with giving nondeterministic agents broad access; permissions must be dynamic. Compliance requires audit trails tying agent actions to humans, complicated by agents acting fast and spawning sub-agents, making observability and enterprise logging critical.

sections.title: Four Architecture Patterns for Agent Identity
sections.summary: Grinich proposes four patterns. Persona shadowing creates scoped shadow identities of users with subset privileges. Delegation chains use signed tokens passed step-by-step, each carrying original user authorization. Capability tokens are self-contained, time-bound vouchers for specific actions, akin to Google's macaroons. Escalation to humans requires approval but risks consent fatigue. He suggests combining patterns depending on the application.

sections.title: Emerging Standards and Protocols for Agent Identity
sections.summary: Grinich surveys emerging standards. OAuth is ubiquitous but built for human consent and static scopes. OIDC came to MCP recently for splitting authorization from resource servers. UMA (User Managed Access) extends OAuth to externalize consent and access policies. GNAP (RFC 9635) enables dynamic token scope negotiation for agents needing unforeseen permissions, but lacks implementation. OIDC for Agents bakes agent identity claims and delegation chains into OIDC. W3C Verifiable Credentials, originally for people, are being adapted for agent identity attestations.

sections.title: Middleware for Agents and What's Next
sections.summary: The dominant industry pattern is middleware—placing a managed trust boundary between agentic code and enterprise systems, treating agents as untrusted due to prompt injection and hijack risks. WorkOS offers OKIT for MCP identity (used by Cursor) and FGA for granular authorization. He references Microsoft workload identities and Cloudflare's MCP auth. He predicts app traffic will flip from ~95% human to ~95% agent, using a ghost kitchen analogy, and calls for collaboration on agent identity standards.

limitations: Human-in-the-loop approval can cause consent fatigue, leading users to approve everything
Pure impersonation gives agents too much power
Existing least-privilege models do not directly apply to nondeterministic agents
OAuth was built for human consent and static scopes, not machine auth
GNAP has strong ideas but low real-world implementation
OIDC for Agents is very early and its formal status is uncertain
Proposed patterns are not prescriptive or complete
quantitativeClaims: AI companies are the fastest-growing segment of WorkOS's customer base
Today about 95% of app traffic is human, 5% automated; Grinich predicts this will flip to ~95% agent traffic
